name: Collecting Emissions Data
title: Collecting Emissions Data
answer: Collecting emissions data means gathering the raw measurements and activity records that let an organization calculate its greenhouse gas footprint across scope 1, scope 2, and scope 3 categories. It covers direct fuel combustion, purchased electricity and heat, and indirect emissions from suppliers, travel, waste, and product use. The work includes identifying data sources, setting collection frequency, and normalizing units such as kilowatt hours, litres of fuel, or tonnes of material into a common carbon equivalent. For an AI accountant, this data is the foundation for audit-ready carbon ledgers and regulatory disclosures.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Collecting emissions data means gathering the raw measurements and activity records that let an organization calculate its greenhouse gas footprint across scope 1, scope 2, and scope 3 categories. It covers direct fuel combustion, purchased electricity and heat, and indirect emissions from suppliers, travel, waste, and product use. The work includes identifying data sources, setting collection frequency, and normalizing units such as kilowatt hours, litres of fuel, or tonnes of material into a common carbon equivalent. For an AI accountant, this data is the foundation for audit-ready carbon ledgers and regulatory disclosures.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Collection runs on a mix of utility meter feeds, building management systems, fleet telematics, supplier invoices, and enterprise resource planning records. Many teams use cloud data warehouses or sustainability platforms to ingest and store the records, with application programming interfaces pulling from energy providers and logistics systems. Spreadsheets still appear at smaller sites, but automated connectors reduce manual entry and improve repeatability. The infrastructure must preserve source timestamps and unit metadata so that later calculations can be traced.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by mapping each activity to an emission factor, then multiplying activity data by that factor to estimate carbon dioxide equivalent. Analysts first define boundaries, then collect primary data where available and use spend based or average data methods for gaps. Quality checks compare current readings against historical ranges and flag missing meters or duplicate invoices. The result is a structured dataset with provenance for every line, ready for verification or external assurance.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on data ownership, confidentiality of supplier and utility records, and the accuracy of estimates used in public reporting. Organizations must document who supplied each figure, when it was collected, and what assumptions or emission factors were applied. Poor provenance can lead to greenwashing claims, audit findings, or contractual disputes if a supplier's reported emissions are later revised. Clear retention rules and access controls protect commercially sensitive energy data while allowing auditors to trace the chain of custody.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Collection is moving toward continuous, machine readable feeds from smart meters, internet connected sensors, and supplier portals rather than annual manual surveys. More companies are asking suppliers for primary activity data instead of spend based estimates, and regulators are pushing for assurance over reported figures. Over time, emissions data may be treated like financial data, with daily or monthly closes, automated anomaly detection, and standardized exchange formats. The AI accountant's role will shift from compiling spreadsheets to governing a live carbon data pipeline.
